title: Humility
hookLine: humility is taking your rightful space, no more and no less
last: ONE MIDDAH GETS THE WHOLE WEEK.

cards: Two people in the same meeting. One talks through every pause, takes every credit, fills every silence. The other sits in the corner with the answer everyone needs and never says it, because who are they to speak?
Ask the room which one is humble, and the corner may well get the vote. Jewish teachers of character would push back: both have the measure wrong. One takes too much space.
The other takes too little, and the room loses what they had to give.

teach.h: MOSES: VERY MEEK, AND NOT SMALL.

teach.b: First, Moses. The Torah, in the book of Numbers, calls Moses very meek, more than anyone on the face of the earth.
That's the same Moses who stood before Pharaoh, carried the tablets down the mountain and argued with God on behalf of his people. So humility here doesn't mean shrinking.
The humblest man in the Torah's own description took up a great deal of room, when the room needed him. Second, the prophet Micah.

teach.h: WALK HUMBLY: A WAY OF MOVING.
teach.b: Asked what God requires, he answers with three things, and the last is to "walk humbly with thy God." Walk: humility as a way of moving through the world, not a feeling about yourself.
Third, two pockets. A story is told about the Hasidic teacher Rabbi Simcha Bunim. He said a person should carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket.
One says: for my sake the world was created, a line from the Mishnah. The other: I am but dust and ashes, Abraham's words in Genesis. The trick is knowing which pocket to reach into.
About to stay silent while someone is wronged? The first. About to take more than your share?

teach.h: NOT TOO LARGE, NOT TOO SMALL.
teach.b: That's why some Mussar teachers describe anavah as being right-sized: not too large, crowding everyone out; not too small, hiding a gift the room needs.
A humble person, in this picture, thinks accurately, then makes room for others. Humility makes a good first trait, because every other trait needs it to stay honest.

how: In Mussar practice, Jews working on anavah watch how much space they take in conversations and in their homes, sometimes keeping the two-pocket teaching of Rabbi Simcha Bunim as a reminder.

o: humility: your right size, no more, no less
thinking as little of yourself as you can
staying silent so others can speak first

p: very meek, and still led a people
for my sake the world was created
I am but dust and ashes

s: humility means thinking little of yourself
in Mussar it means being right-sized: not too large, not too small.
the Torah calls Moses very meek
in the book of Numbers, the same Moses who faced Pharaoh.
staying silent while someone is wronged counts as humble
that's the moment for the first pocket: for my sake the world was created.

games.q: you carry two slips of paper. you're about to take more than your share. which pocket do you reach into?
o: for my sake the world was created.
I am but dust and ashes.
neither; humility is a feeling, not a habit.
games.why: as the story is told, Rabbi Simcha Bunim's second slip, dust and ashes, is for the moment you're about to take too much.

practice: Start with your body: let your seat be just what you need, feet on the floor, back long, shoulders easy.

Picture your next conversation and ask which pocket you'll need: if you usually swallow something true, picture saying it plainly; if you usually take over, picture leaving one pause open for someone else.
If you pray, carry this before God in your own words; if not, simply sit right-sized, and let that be enough.

wordCard.voice: Anavah. Humility: in Mussar, being right-sized, taking the space that is yours, no more and no less. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: humility. the Torah calls Moses anav, meek.

carryVoice: Your line: right-sized. Not too large to crowd others out, not too small to give. Until tomorrow.
